title: Why We Like to Believe Other People Are Stupid
author: Stafford, Tom
summary: Tom Stafford examines why media and researchers systematically favor results that make human beings look irrational, credulous, and biased -- what he calls the 'people are stupid' school of psychology. The piece builds on an analysis of the Lizardman constant in surveys (the consistent small percentage who endorse absurd propositions) to argue that inauthentic survey responding, not actual belief in lizard people, drives many alarming statistics. A key example: Kahneman's Thinking Fast and Slow is a careful book, but even Kahneman sometimes implies Fast Thinking is biased and Slow Thinking is rational -- a distortion the media then amplifies. Stafford argues that cognitive science research is selected and transmitted in ways that emphasize human foolishness, because such findings are shareable and satisfying -- they confirm the audience's sense of being more rational than the masses. The article is ultimately an epistemological corrective: before accepting research that paints human cognition as disastrously flawed, ask whether the finding might reflect survey methodology, media selection bias, or the social pleasures of believing others are stupid.
points: The 'people are stupid' school distorts cognitive science: research emphasizing human irrationality gets disproportionate media attention, while findings showing reasonableness or adaptive cognition are de-emphasized in subsequent citations.

The Lizardman constant -- the small but consistent percentage of respondents who endorse absurd propositions -- is primarily an artifact of inauthentic responding (people answering for fun or not reading questions) rather than evidence of widespread bizarre beliefs.

Even Kahneman's Thinking Fast and Slow, a balanced and careful work, slips into implying Fast Thinking is biased and Slow Thinking is rational -- a simplification that gets amplified into a misleading popular story about dual-process cognition.

A key mechanism: stories showing human foolishness are more shareable and socially rewarding than stories showing human rationality, which creates systematic selection pressure in media coverage of psychology research.

Stafford's corrective: before accepting alarming claims about human irrationality, investigators should ask whether the finding reflects genuine cognition or methodological artifacts, researcher incentives, or the social pleasures of elite audiences enjoying evidence that ordinary people are irrational.
quotes: The book is a magnificent synthesis of work in the judgement and decision tradition, a tradition which the author helped found and define. The Fast Thinking of the title is intuitive and based on pattern recognition, the Slow Thinking is deliberate and reasoned.

Perhaps it is true, failures are more interesting, so it is understandable why more attention is devoted to them, but that doesn't mean they define the majority of human attempts at reasoning, nor that biased or unsuccessful reasoning is the product of a single type of process (and there is some kind of better reasoning process 'underneath' which remains untapped). When Kahneman's work is talked about by others there is sometimes another distortion -- bias and rationality become properties of individuals, rather than properties of processes which we all possess.

Maybe it is no more than attentional bias to bad news [ ] -- just as stories of crime and disaster invite us to prepare for life-threatening dangers, so stories of foolishness and error invite us to prepare for reason-threatening dangers. Better to overestimate the chances of error than be wrong with a false confidence.

We know these better for ourselves than for other people, but it is easy to neglect our ignorance of the differences in environment, information and motivation between us and others. When we observe other people's choices we conclude people are making them for our environment, with the knowledge we have, for the reasons we make decisions.

The belief also seems to feed fairly directly into anti-democratic sentiment. If people are fools then they shouldn't be trusted to make decisions about society, and maybe it is better to let an (intellectual) elite decide instead.
The citation bias: Fad and fashion in the judgment and decision literature. That paper on measuring belief in the reasonableness of others: Stafford, T., Zhu, J., & Dommett, K. (2024, December 31).
